summary: Find bugs in the LUCID camera, long-flight and real-map builder code; adversarially verify each finding

result.title: GUI mode renders every 5 ms physics step, so the 262 s straight flight needs about 52,000 RTX frames
result.scenario: `--route straight --view chase` (the documented GUI command), or `--view front` without `--record`. `cams` is empty, so `sim.step(render=capture or not cams)` renders on every 0.005 s step. The flight lasts about 262 s of sim time, which is about 52,400 rendered frames of the 2 km map. At a realistic 15-30 fps the drone is 7-13x slower than real time. At 10 m/s cruise it appears to move at about 1 m/s, and one lap takes roughly 30-60 minutes. The recording path avoids this by rendering only every 8th step (`every`).
result.evidence: Read lines 561-569 and the Isaac Lab `SimulationContext.step`. The Isaac Sim 5.1.0 source for `step(render=True)` calls `self._app.update()` once per physics step. The dt is 0.005, `render_interval` is 1, and `rendering_dt` equals the physics dt, so neither dt is zero. Arithmetic: 262 s / 0.005 s = 52,400. I did not run the GUI because Isaac Sim is not available here.
result.fix: In GUI mode render only every `every`-th step. For example, set `render = (count % every == 0)` for the flight routes, not `capture or not cams`. Call `chase.update` and `sim.set_camera_view` only on those steps, with dt = `every * sim_dt`. Keep render-every-step only for the hover demo, which has a 20 s loop.

verdict.reasoning: The reported bug does not exist in the code under review. The claim is that the loop calls `sim.step(render=capture or not cams)`, so GUI flights render on every 5 ms physics step. The code at lines 571-582 of quadcopter_pbr.py is different. It sets `capture = bool(cams) and count % every == 0`, then `render_now = capture if cams else (fl is None or count % every == 0)`, then calls `sim.step(render=render_now)`. With `--route straight --view chase`, `cams` is empty and `fl` is not None, so `render_now` is `count % every == 0`. `every = round(1/(fps*sim_dt))` = 8 at the default 25 fps and 0.005 s, so the GUI renders every 8th step (25 fps), which is real time. Only the hover demo (`fl is None`) renders every step, which matches the reviewer's own suggested fix. The chase camera update and `sim.set_camera_view` are also gated on `render_now`, and they use `dt = sim_dt * every`, which is also what the reviewer suggested. A comment at lines 572-573 says the same thing. `git show HEAD` shows this fix is already committed in d1ad8dd ("Isaac review fixes: GUI flights in real time, chase camera at its real distance"), and the working-tree diff has no change to that logic. `grep render=` shows no other `render=capture or not cams` call. In Isaac Lab, `SimulationContext.step(render=False)` only steps physics, so skipping the render on the other 7 of 8 steps works as intended. The reviewer was probably reading an older version.
verdict.repro: Read /home/user/vla-datagen/scripts/drone_scene/quadcopter_pbr.py lines 440-639, covering `every`, `capture`, `render_now`, the chase update and `sim.step(render=render_now)`. Ran `grep -n "render=\|render_now"` on the working tree and on `git show HEAD:scripts/drone_scene/quadcopter_pbr.py`; the `render_now` logic is identical in both and no `capture or not cams` expression exists. Checked `git diff HEAD` for render changes, and found none. Read `SimulationContext.step` in /home/user/vla-datagen/source/isaaclab/isaaclab/sim/simulation_context.py and found it passes `render` to `super().step`, so `render=False` skips rendering. Did not run Isaac Sim, which is not available here.

result.title: Chase camera sits about 18 m behind the drone at cruise, not the nominal 10 m, so the drone is a ~40 px speck
result.scenario: `--cameras chase` or `--view chase` on the straight route. `ChaseCamera` low-pass filters the eye towards `p - direction*back + up` with a 0.8 s time constant. A first-order lag behind a target moving at v leaves a steady-state offset of v*tau = 8 m. At 10 m/s the camera therefore ends up about 18 m behind instead of the 10 m of `back=10`. The chase video shows a 0.52 m drone only about 42 px wide in the 1280 px frame during the 200+ s cruise. It is 75 px wide while stationary or climbing.
result.evidence: I copied `ChaseCamera` and ran it over `StraightFlight` at the camera frame step (dt=0.04). Eye-to-drone distance was 10.1 m at t=5 s (climb) and 18.1 m at t=60 s and t=100 s (cruise). Apparent drone width at 47.3 deg HFOV on 1280 px was 75 px, then 42 px.
result.fix: Add velocity feed-forward so the lag does not push the camera back. Compute `want = p - direction*back + up`, then `self.eye += (want + v*self.lag - self.eye)*a`. Alternatively smooth only the lateral and vertical error, or use a smaller `back` such as 6 m and a longer `lag_s`.

verdict.reasoning:
The reported lag is real for the older code, but the code under review already contains the fix, so the bug does not happen. In /home/user/vla-datagen/scripts/drone_scene/quadcopter_pbr.py (lines 316-333) `ChaseCamera.update(p, v, direction, dt)` now has the velocity feed-forward the reviewer suggests: `self.eye += (want + v*self.lag - self.eye)*a`. The caller at line 576 passes `fl.velocity(t)`. The fix is in commit d1ad8dd ("Isaac review fixes: GUI flights in real time, chase camera at its real distance"). That commit's docstring describes the same problem: "a plain first-order lag would trail speed x lag further back (18 m instead of 10 m at 10 m/s)". The working tree has no further change to this class.

I ran the current `ChaseCamera` over `StraightFlight` at dt=0.04 with the default 10 m/s cruise. Eye-to-drone distance stayed between 10.4 and 10.6 m for the whole flight:

| Time | Distance |
|---|---|
| t=5 s (climb) | 10.6 m |
| t=60 to 200 s (cruise) | 10.41 m |
| t=242 s | 10.58 m |
| t=257 s | 10.59 m |

The cruise offset is -7.83, -5.90 horizontally and +3.5 m up, against a nominal 10 m back and 3.5 m up. The extra ~0.4 m comes from `direction` being horizontal while the drag tilt makes the velocity slightly different. That is negligible, and the drone's apparent width is about 72 px, not 42 px.

For comparison, I also ran a plain first-order lag with the feed-forward removed. It gave 18.14 m at cruise, which matches the reviewer's number. That is the behaviour the fix removed. Apparent size follows 1/distance, so the cruise drone is now about 7% smaller than at hover.
verdict.repro: Read quadcopter_pbr.py lines 316-333, 538 and 575-581. Ran `git log -p -S"velocity feed-forward"`, which shows the fix added in commit d1ad8dd. Wrote /tmp/claude-0/review/chase.py, which extracts the current `ChaseCamera` from the file, drives it over `flight.StraightFlight(heading_deg=37)` at dt=0.04, and compares it with a no-feed-forward variant. Result: 18.14 m at cruise without feed-forward (the claimed bug) and 10.41 m with the current code.

result.title: `--record -1` (the documented whole-flight command) creates no cameras and never exits
result.scenario: The README's main straight-route command is `--route straight --headless --record -1 --cameras front back chase`, and the flag help says -1 means the whole flight. Both `if args_cli.record > 0` guards are false for -1: line 170 does not set enable_cameras, and line 445 skips creating the Camera sensors. `cams` stays empty, so the exit test `if cams and count >= record_steps` (line 599) never fires. The headless run steps and renders forever, writes no mp4 and no camera_info.json, and never logs 'recording ...'. `seconds = fl.duration` and `record_steps` are computed but never used.
result.evidence: Read lines 60-61, 170, 445, 506-509 and 599, and README.md line 96. In a headless run `simulation_app.is_running()` stays true, so nothing ends the loop. Not run here (Isaac Sim is unavailable), but the control flow is unambiguous.
result.fix: Use `args_cli.record != 0` at both line 170 and line 445, so -1 enables cameras and recording. Reject -1 when there is no flight (`fl is None`), because `seconds` would be -1 and the loop would stop after one frame.

verdict.reasoning:
The reported defect is not present in the current tree. The reviewer's guards (`if args_cli.record > 0` at line 170 and the matching check at line 445) were replaced in commit ea62ab2 ("Review fixes: --record -1"), which is an ancestor of HEAD d1ad8dd. The working tree is clean. In the current code:
- Line 170-171 rejects a negative --record when there is no flight (`parser.error`, so `fl is None` with -1 is handled).
- Line 172 sets `RECORDING = args_cli.record != 0`, so -1 counts as recording. Line 173-174 then sets `enable_cameras`.
- The camera creation block at line 455 is `if RECORDING:`, so `cams` is filled for `--record -1 --cameras front back chase`.
- Line 516 sets `seconds = fl.duration if (record < 0 and fl is not None) else record`. `record_steps` is used by the exit test `if cams and count >= record_steps: break` at line 611-612. So -1 stops at the end of the flight, then writes the mp4 and camera_info.json and exits via `os._exit`.
- `fl = geom if args_cli.fly else None` (line 425). `--route straight` forces `fly = True` (line 104-105). Both flight classes define `.duration`.
- A non-flight run with -1 now fails fast with a parser error instead of stopping after one frame.
The reviewer probably read the version before ea62ab2.
verdict.repro: I did not run the Isaac script, since Isaac Sim is not available here. I read quadcopter_pbr.py lines 55-190 and 425-640 and grepped for `record`, `RECORDING` and `fl =`. I ran `git status`, `git log` and `git show ea62ab2`, which shows the diff turning `if args_cli.record > 0:` into `RECORDING = args_cli.record != 0` plus the parser.error guard. I also checked `duration` in flight.py for Flight and StraightFlight.

result.title: Map terrain is coplanar with the backyard patio at z=0 and sits above the scene's lawn and mulch bed
result.scenario: The take-off pad is flattened to z_take = 0.0 (lines 381 and 134-136), exactly the scene's `patio_top = 0.0`. The 3D pavers have tops at 0 +/- 1.65 mm (height jitter plus tilt, see `PaverSpec.top_rise`), and the sand is at 0.0. Roughly half of the paver tops are therefore buried under the map terrain, and the rest stand at most 1.7 mm proud, so the patio the drone 'takes off from' mostly shows the terrain's lawn texture. `scene.build` is not told about the map. Its lawn (z = -0.025) and mulch bed (top = -0.013) lie entirely below the terrain, so the bed is invisible. The take-off, the first seconds in `front`/`back` and the whole climb show a broken patio.
result.evidence: Opened the built world.usdc: the vertices of /Map/Terrain with |x| and |y| < 3 m are exactly z = 0.0, apart from the -2 m skirt. Read scene.py: `patio_top: 0.0`, `lawn_z: -0.025`, bed top `lawn_z + 0.012`, curb top 0.008. `pavers.hide_flat_patio`'s own docstring says coplanar surfaces z-fight the bricks. quadcopter_pbr.scene_cfg() leaves patio_top and lawn_z unchanged for WORLD.
result.fix: Put the map terrain under the backyard: use a take-off pad height below the lawn slab (at most about -0.08 m), or cut the terrain out under the lawn. Then compute the landing clearance in make_flight from the gear offset (`robot_z0 - cfg.patio_top`), not `start_z - WORLD['takeoff']['z']`, which would otherwise leave the drone hovering about 8 cm over the landing grass.

verdict.reasoning:
The report describes an older version of the code. At HEAD d1ad8dd the take-off pad is no longer at z=0.0. build.py:441-446 sets `z_take = SceneCfg().lawn_z`, which is -0.025 m, with a comment that the pad is flattened to the backyard's lawn level so the patio, curb and mulch bed stand on it. This was done in commit 52b1f79, whose message says the map terrain is the lawn there and that the mulch bed is not buried. The line numbers (build.py:381, 134-136) and the description "z_take = 0.0" do not match the current file.

With the terrain at -0.025 m, the scene geometry stacks as follows:
- Patio top is 0.0, so it stands 25 mm above the terrain. Paver tops at 0 +/- 1.65 mm are therefore well clear of it.
- Bed top is lawn_z + 0.012 = -0.013, so it stands 12 mm above the terrain.
- Curb top is 0.008 m, also above the terrain.
- The hand-built lawn quad is shrunk to lawn_half = 0.5 on the world route (quadcopter_pbr.scene_cfg). It lies entirely under the patio, which spans x -1.6..2.0 and y -2.2..2.0 with top at 0, so any coplanarity with the terrain at -0.025 is hidden.

The reviewer's suggested landing-clearance fix is also already in place. `make_flight(onboard, start_z, clearance)` takes the gear clearance directly: `clearance = 0.005 - z_feet`, passed as `ground_clearance`. Grep finds no remaining use of `start_z - WORLD['takeoff']['z']`, so the landing height is end_ground_z + gear offset and the drone does not hover over the grass.

I confirmed with a scratch script (/tmp/claude-0/review/t1.py) that `terrain.tile_mesh` with the current `_pads(SceneCfg().lawn_z, ...)` puts every terrain vertex with |x|,|y| < 3 m at exactly -0.025.

The only place a z=0 take-off survives is the stale cached world.usdc under the scratchpad (world_5371363afc, takeoff z=0.0, built with BUILD_VERSION "1" on 2026-10-17 23:50). That is where the reviewer's observation of z=0 vertices came from. BUILD_VERSION is now "4" and is part of the cache key (`_key`), so the current code will not reuse that stale map. It rebuilds into a different directory with the fixed pad height.
verdict.repro: Read build.py (lines 120-150, 190-300, 425-450), scene.py (SceneCfg, author_ground, box), quadcopter_pbr.py (scene_cfg, make_flight, main) and terrain.py (Pad, apply_pads, tile_mesh). Ran git log -S to see that `z_take = SceneCfg().lawn_z` came in with commit 52b1f79, before HEAD. Compared the stale world.json (takeoff z=0.0, version 1) with BUILD_VERSION="4" in the cache key. Ran /tmp/claude-0/review/t1.py with the scratchpad venv: terrain vertices within 3 m of the origin are all at -0.025.

result.title: Onboard cameras see the drone's own lower plate: bottom ~9% of the back frame and both lower corners of the front frame
result.scenario: `mount_cameras` only looks at body vertices inside a thin height band around the camera axis, so it misses structure below the lens that falls inside the pitched-down view cone. In the LMF2's base_link mesh (magpie_lowres), a plate ~16-17 cm wide and ~1 cm thick (z = 5-15 mm) ends at x = -0.268 at the tail and at x = +0.247 at the nose. The back lens sits at x = -0.20, z = 0.095, only ~9 cm from the plate. At the default 20 deg pitch the plate is 29-33 deg below the optical axis, so it fills the bottom ~9% of the 69 deg vertical field of view across the full width. The front camera gets two blobs in its lower left and right corners (18-28 deg below the axis, about 4% of the frame). It stays at that spot in every frame, at 9-12 cm from the lens and out of focus. At 10 deg pitch (garden) it is the bottom ~10% of the back frame and the front corners.
result.evidence: Loaded the cached arl_robot_1.usd and ran `vehicles.mount_cameras` on its base_link vertices (all 1.1 M points). Projected every triangle through the render-plan pinhole and rasterised it: at 20 deg the back camera has coverage 0.12 of the render frame (rows 395-449 of 450), and the front has two lower-corner blobs. 105 vertices of magpie_lowres lie in the front camera's frustum, the nearest at 0.10 m. The saved rasters are /tmp/claude-0/review/view_back_20.png and view_front_20.png.
result.fix: When choosing the mount, also test body vertices against the camera's pitched viewing cone (lens front back to the near plane). Move the lens out or up until no body vertex falls inside it, or mount the lens beyond the plate edge.

verdict.reasoning: The claim describes a version of mount_cameras that no longer exists. In the code at HEAD, mount_cameras takes a `triangles` argument. For each candidate mount it calls view_blocked(), which draws the drone's own triangles through the real lens (distortion included, clipped at the near plane). It rejects mounts that cover more than 1% of the view and moves the camera up or out until the view is clear. The user's script, quadcopter_pbr.py:414-415, calls it as `vehicles.mount_cameras(pts, RIG, VEHICLE.camera_z, pitch_down_deg=CAMERA_PITCH, triangles=vehicles.body_triangles(stage, body))`. The reviewer's repro called `mount_cameras(V, rig, 0.06, pitch_down_deg=pitch)` with no `triangles`, which falls back to the vertex-band collision rule only. That is not the real call path. Commit ea62ab2 ("self-free camera mounts") added the triangle check for exactly this problem; its message mentions the 10-12% back-view panel coverage the reviewer found. I reran the repro on the cached arl_robot_1.usd with an independent exact raster of all 368,635 triangles under base_link, collision meshes included. The raster is a pinhole through the render plan and does not use view_blocked. Without triangles it reproduces the reviewer's numbers: back camera 12.05% covered at 20 deg and 10.4% at 10 deg, front 3-4%, with the back lens at x=-0.200, z=0.095. With triangles, as the script actually calls it, coverage is 0.0000 for both cameras at 20 deg. At 10 deg the back camera is 0.0000 and the front is 0.0030. The mount moves to back x=-0.220 at 20 deg and -0.201, z=0.107 at 10 deg; front x=0.182, z=0.075 at 20 deg and x=0.169 at 10 deg. test_vehicles.py (13 tests, including TestRealLMF2, which asserts view_blocked <= 0.01 for both cameras at 10 and 20 deg) passes. The bug does not occur on the user's setup.
verdict.repro: Read vehicles.py (mount_cameras, view_blocked, body_triangles) and the call site in quadcopter_pbr.py lines 411-415. Checked git log: ea62ab2 added the triangle-based self-view check. Wrote /tmp/claude-0/review/refute_mount.py, which loads /root/.cache/drone_scene/Isaac/Robots/NTNU/ARL-Robot-1/arl_robot_1.usd, runs mount_cameras with and without triangles at 10 and 20 deg, and rasterises all body triangles independently. Without triangles the output matches the reviewer (back 0.1205 and 0.1036, front ~0.03-0.04); with triangles it is 0.0000 except front 0.0030 at 10 deg. Ran scripts/drone_scene/test/test_vehicles.py: 13 tests OK.

result.title: GUI chase camera stops following the drone after the first lap
result.scenario: With `--route straight --view chase` (README example 3, interactive), the drone's time wraps every `fl.duration + 2` s (line 536). The chase camera uses the unwrapped `t = min(count * sim_dt, fl.duration)` (line 555). After about 267 s the drone restarts its take-off in the backyard, but the chase eye stays at the landing spot 2 km away, looking at the final position.
result.evidence: Read lines 534-562: the two time computations differ once `count * sim_dt > fl.duration + 2` and `cams` is empty. The StraightFlight duration for the Ames map is 264.9 s.
result.fix: Compute the wrapped time once and use it for both the drone and the chase camera. Reset `chase.eye` (set it to None) when the lap restarts.

verdict.reasoning:
The claimed mismatch between the drone time and the chase-camera time does not exist in the code. The reviewer says the chase camera uses a separate unwrapped `t = min(count * sim_dt, fl.duration)`. In `/home/user/vla-datagen/scripts/drone_scene/quadcopter_pbr.py` (HEAD, file unmodified in the working tree), `t` is computed once at lines 546-547 as `t = (count*sim_dt) % (fl.duration+2.0) if not cams else count*sim_dt`, then `t = min(t, fl.duration)`. The chase block at line 568 calls `chase.update(fl.position(t), fl.velocity(t), fl.direction, ...)` with that same `t`. There is no second `t` computation, and the cited line numbers (536, 555) hold unrelated code. In the `--route straight --view chase` GUI case, `cams` is empty, so `t` wraps for both the drone and the chase camera. After a wrap, `fl.position(t)` is back in the backyard, so the chase target and the `want` position follow it. `ChaseCamera.update` (lines 315-325) recomputes `want` from the current drone position every call and moves the eye toward it with an exponential lag, so the eye cannot stay at the landing spot.

One related effect exists, but it is not the reported bug. `ChaseCamera.eye` is not reset at the wrap, so the eye starts about 2 km from the new take-off. I simulated the update formula with a 0.8 s lag and a ~33 Hz update. The eye closes the 2 km gap in about 6 s (residual 2.3 m at 5.4 s, 0.7 m at 6.3 s). So the interactive loop shows a brief fast swoop back across the map at each lap restart, then the camera follows correctly. That is a cosmetic glitch, not "stops following after the first lap". Recording mode never wraps, so it is unaffected.
verdict.repro: Read quadcopter_pbr.py lines 440-620 and ChaseCamera (lines 308-325). Checked `git diff HEAD` (no changes to the file) and `git show HEAD:...` lines 540-575, which match the working tree and contain no `min(count * sim_dt, ...)` expression. Ran /tmp/claude-0/review/chase_wrap.py, which simulates the ChaseCamera lag from a 2000 m offset; the eye converges to within 1 m in about 6 s.
verdict.better_fix: Not needed. Optionally set `chase.eye = None` when `t` wraps in the GUI loop, so the camera snaps to the take-off instead of swooping 2 km at each lap restart.

result.title: Garden tour yaw snaps (3.4 deg and 6.9 deg in one physics step) where the speed crosses 0.25 m/s
result.scenario: `Flight.heading` switches to `velocity(1 s)` or `velocity(duration - 1 s)` whenever the horizontal speed is below 0.25 m/s, and switches back to the real direction above it. That is a discontinuity in yaw. At t = 0.52 s the yaw steps 3.4 deg in one 5 ms step. At t = 19.57 s it steps 6.9 deg (an instantaneous rate of 1376 deg/s), so the last frames of both onboard videos jerk sideways.
result.evidence: Ran Flight().heading on a 5 ms grid: the only steps above 0.5 deg are at t = 0.52 (3.4 deg) and t = 19.57 (6.88 deg, speed 0.252 m/s). Yaw is -30.8 deg at the start, the actual direction at the threshold differs, and it is -23.5 deg at the end.
result.fix: Blend the yaw instead of switching: for example, a smoothstep between the borrowed heading and the actual one as speed goes from 0.1 to 0.5 m/s. Or hold the last well-defined heading and use an angle-unwrapped low-pass filter.

verdict.reasoning: The reported bug does not exist in the current code. The claim says `Flight.heading` hard-switches to a borrowed heading (`velocity(1 s)` or `velocity(duration - 1 s)`) when horizontal speed is below 0.25 m/s. The code at flight.py:145-152 does something else. It computes `v + max(0, 0.5 - |v|) * ref`, where `ref` is the unit direction of travel 1 s inside the flight. That is a continuous blend with weight (0.5 - |v|), fading to zero at 0.5 m/s. There is no 0.25 m/s threshold and no branch. The function is continuous in t, so it has no yaw discontinuity. The commit "ea62ab2 Review fixes ... garden heading" appears to have already replaced the switch the reviewer describes. `git status` shows flight.py has no uncommitted changes. I ran `Flight().heading` on a 5 ms grid over the whole 20 s flight. The largest yaw step is 0.46 deg, at t = 5.48 s, which is ordinary turning through the path's curved section. No step exceeds 0.5 deg, and the 3.4 deg step at t = 0.52 s and the 6.9 deg step at t = 19.57 s do not occur. Around the cited times the yaw is smooth: -29.09 deg at both t = 0.50 and t = 0.52, and -19.93 deg then -19.99 deg at t = 19.5 and t = 19.57. The 92 deg/s peak yaw rate is real path curvature, not a snap. Sampling at 30 and 60 fps gives maximum per-frame steps of 3.07 and 1.53 deg. These come from the same smooth turn near t = 5.5 s, so they are not the claimed jerk at the start and end of the videos.
verdict.repro: Read /home/user/vla-datagen/scripts/drone_scene/flight.py (heading at lines 145-152, blend form). Ran /tmp/claude-0/review/yaw.py with the scratchpad venv python. It evaluated Flight().heading over 0..20 s at 5 ms, 1/30 s and 1/60 s, and unwrapped the yaw to find step sizes. Result: max step 0.46 deg at t = 5.48 s, no step above 0.5 deg, and smooth yaw near t = 0.5 s and t = 19.57 s. Checked git log and status: flight.py is committed, with the garden-heading fix in ea62ab2.

result.title: Pitched roofs leave footprint areas unroofed (up to 10 percent by design, wings and notches open to the sky)
result.scenario: cover_rectangles stops as soon as 10 percent or less of the footprint is uncovered (`left.sum() > 0.1 * total`), takes at most 4 rectangles, and gives up when the next rectangle is under 12 m2. Walls are still built on the whole outline (double-sided, no floor), so a garage wing, bay or L-notch is a hole in the roof through which the interior or ground shows from the drone camera. Hip and gable roofs never cover those parts.
result.evidence: Parsed the built world.usdc: the 18,932 buildings split cleanly into wall ring plus roof faces. Union of upward-facing roof triangles intersected with the wall outline: mean coverage 0.980, 15.7 percent of buildings (2,972) below 0.95, 418 below 0.90, 49 below 0.80; 3,031 buildings have more than 10 m2 unroofed. Same numbers on the second build (world_fbc512c47f). A top-down plot of 12 low-coverage houses shows uncovered wings and corners.
result.fix: Keep covering until about 1-2 percent is left, with max_rects about 6 and min_area about 3 m2, and roof any remainder (footprint minus the union of the rectangles plus overhang) with a lean-to or flat patch at eave height.

verdict.reasoning: The claim describes code that is no longer in the branch. The reviewer measured world_5371363afc (world.json version 1) and world_fbc512c47f (version 2). Both were built before commit 951bc95 ("pitched roofs: cover the footprint to 98 % with up to 6 rectangles and give the rest a flat roof"). That commit changed cover_rectangles from max_rects=4, min_area=12, `left.sum() > 0.1*total` to max_rects=6, min_area=3.0, leave=0.02. It also added _flat_remainder, which roofs whatever the rectangles leave (footprint minus the rectangle union buffered 0.05 m) with a flat patch at eave+0.02, and building_mesh calls it. This is the reviewer's own suggested fix, already applied at buildings.py lines 145-156 and 303-304. BUILD_VERSION is now "5", so the user's cache key changes and the map is rebuilt with the fixed code. Re-running the reviewer's measurement on the current code gives full coverage. I took 2,046 real Overture footprints from the Ames detail zone, 1,969 of them pitched, and ran the current building_mesh. The union of upward-facing roof triangles covers the footprint with mean 1.0000 and minimum 0.998. No building has coverage below 0.99, and none has more than 1 m2 unroofed. The same measurement with the old parameters (rectangles only) gives mean 0.982 and 12.7 percent of buildings below 0.95. That matches the reviewer's numbers, so the method is sound and the bug existed in the old code but is fixed now.

The corner R-B fringe is therefore smaller than the datasheet-style value in Lens (documented as the red-blue separation at the image corner, in pixels). It is wrong by about 13 percent for the default C4 lens and 23 percent for the strongly distorted S3.6.

For example derive the undistorted corner radius and the local d(render px)/d(output px) from xu, yu and plan['fx'], and set half = 0.5*lateral_color_px*jac / (r_u_corner_px_render).
